I have an plastic injection mold machine in my shop. Let me run the economics by you.

  • First of all, the molds are insanely expensive for a full production run. We are talking $5000 minimum for the smallest most irrelevant part.

  • But, before you get there, you need to pay the game designers to design each figure.

  • Then you have to pay someone 3D model each character in a CAD program.

  • Then you have to pay someone to program the mill to carve out the mold.

So, now you just spent probably upwards of $1,000,000 just for molds for this year's newest figures... And you still don't have any actual product.

  • So, now you need to fly to China to get a contract with a company that specializes in limited runs. That is expensive, because you are basically paying rent for all that factory's upkeep while they are doing your production run. So, you are paying for their electricity, utilities, pay for each worker, overhead, etc. Probably for a whole month. That could easily be $1,000,000 minimum.

  • Then you have to pay your own people back in your own home office. Pay the utilities, pay for packaging. Pay for marketing.

  • Now consider, you have all this inventory that hasn't been sold yet. So, you need to warehouse it.

  • Then you need to pay for global shipping.

  • Now consider that not everything will sell at once. So, you'll slowly chew through your inventory. But, you won't fully get a return on your investment until it is ALL sold, which can take years. Meanwhile, your investors probably gave you a line of credit to cover all this overhead and interest is piling up.

  • And finally, there is the bitch. Supply and demand. There are only so many nerds. It's a limited market. So, low demands dictates a low supply. Which means all this overhead cost is split among a product that each nerd is only going to need 1 or 2 of any given figure and 100's of SKU's.

And that's the kicker. The number of SKU's. If Warhammer only had maybe a dozen total figures, they could make them SUPER cheap. But, it's a SKU heavy franchise. That's why what seems like a 1¢ figure costs $10.

And that's why I bought my own plastic injection mold.

GW do their moldmaking and molding in-house, so they're not paying contractor rates. Also it's not like they're producing the most complicated and expensive multi-part molds with cooling and hot runners etc, they're just regular two part molds.

Given their volume of sales their fixed costs (mold production and design, salaries etc.) dwindle to nothing. They managed for years on much lower prices, the current price hikes are pure greed, and they've shown that this is the case with their sale prices.

Global shipping isn't included in their prices, you pay for that on top of the $15 for five minis.

I'm working on starting an injection molding company myself, and what keeps me going is the fact that costs are nowhere near what would be needed to justify GW's prices.

If they are doing injection molding in-house, they are probably saving a little money, maybe 25%, but if they are doing it out of China, then that's probably going to negate any savings. I don't know what their specific situation is, so I can't really say.

But, regardless, it's the supply-demand thing that really raises the prices. One nerd needs maybe 100 figures and maybe 30 of those figures are going to be unique SKUs. That's the thing that really raises the price here.
